title: How to Build a Real Estate Investing Team That Scales With You
excerpt: Building the right team is the difference between doing a few deals a year and running a true real estate business. Learn who to hire, when to hire them, and how to structure your team for long-term growth.
author: AIWholesail Team
tags: how to build a real estate investing team
metaDescription: Learn how to build a real estate investing team step by step. Discover who to hire first, how to find reliable partners, and when to scale your crew.

sections.content: Most real estate investors start out doing everything themselves. You find the leads, run the numbers, talk to sellers, negotiate contracts, coordinate closings, and manage buyers. That works fine at first. But if you want to grow beyond 1 or 2 deals a month, you need people around you. Learning how to build a real estate investing team is one of the most important skills you can develop. It's also what separates a solo side hustle from a real, scalable business. If you're serious about growth, check out our [Scaling a Real Estate Investing Business: Complete Guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/scaling-real-estate-investing-business) for a full roadmap.
Why a Team Changes Everything

There are only 24 hours in a day. When you try to handle acquisitions, dispositions, marketing, and operations on your own, you hit a wall. Deals slip through. Follow-ups get missed. You burn out. A team multiplies your capacity without multiplying your hours. Investors who scale from 1 deal per month to 10 or more almost always have a core team in place. The goal is not to hire a bunch of people at once. It's to add the right person at the right time, so each hire pays for itself. Read more about making that jump in [How to Go From 1 to 10 Deals Per Month](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/scaling-wholesale-deals-per-month).
The Core Roles in a Real Estate Investing Team

Every successful investing operation has a few key functions that need to be covered. In the beginning, you cover all of them. As you grow, you start delegating. Here are the core roles to think about as you build your team.
1. Acquisitions Manager

This is usually the first real hire for a wholesaler or flipper. An acquisitions manager talks to motivated sellers, sets appointments, runs comps, and gets contracts signed. A good acquisitions rep can handle 20 to 40 seller conversations per week. You pay them a flat fee per closed deal, typically $2,000 to $5,000 depending on your market and deal size. In high-volume markets like [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga) or [Dallas](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), a strong acquisitions person can be the difference between 2 and 8 deals a month.
2. Disposition Manager

A disposition manager handles the buyer side. They market your deals to cash buyers, manage negotiations, and push contracts to closing. Once you have a solid buyer list, a skilled dispo person can move deals in 48 to 72 hours. They often work on commission, earning 10% to 20% of the assignment fee per deal. This role is especially valuable in fast-moving markets like [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az) where speed matters.
3. Transaction Coordinator

A transaction coordinator, or TC, manages the paperwork and timeline from contract to close. They follow up with title companies, lenders, and attorneys so nothing falls through the cracks. This role is often part-time at first and can be outsourced for $300 to $600 per deal. A good TC protects your earnest money, keeps closing dates on track, and frees you from inbox overwhelm.
4. Marketing Manager or VA

Someone needs to keep your lead pipeline full. This might be a virtual assistant who runs your direct mail campaigns, manages your CRM, pulls lists, or handles cold calling. Offshore VAs can cost $5 to $15 per hour, while a US-based marketing manager might run $40,000 to $60,000 per year. Start lean with a VA and level up as your deal volume justifies it. Keeping that pipeline organized is critical — see our guide on [Deal Pipeline Management for Real Estate Investors](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/deal-pipeline-management) for best practices.
5. Contractor or Rehab Manager

If you flip or hold rentals, you need reliable contractors. One trusted general contractor who communicates well and hits timelines is worth more than five cheap bids that fall apart. Build relationships with a GC who has a full crew. Pay them fairly and they'll prioritize your projects. This relationship takes time, but it's one of the highest-value connections you can make.

Pro Tip: Before hiring a full-time acquisitions manager, test candidates by paying them per appointment set for 30 days. This shows you their hustle level and communication skills before you commit to a salary or per-deal structure.
Outside Your Core Team: Key Power Partners

Your internal team handles operations. But you also need a reliable network of outside professionals. Think of these as your extended team. Every serious investor needs a real estate attorney, a title company that understands investor transactions, a hard money lender, and a CPA who specializes in real estate. These partners do not work for you full time, but they need to be in place and responsive. A title company that takes three weeks to close will kill your deals. A hard money lender who pulls funding at the last minute will ruin your reputation. Vet these relationships just like you would a full-time hire.
"Your network is your net worth. In real estate, the investor with the best team wins more deals than the investor with the best marketing." — Common wisdom in the wholesaling community
How to Find Good Team Members

The best team members often come from your existing network. Real estate meetups, investor Facebook groups, BiggerPockets forums, and local REIA events are great places to start. When hiring acquisitions or dispo reps, look for people with sales backgrounds, not necessarily real estate experience. Coachability matters more than credentials at this stage. Post on Indeed or LinkedIn using clear job descriptions that emphasize commission-based earnings and the deal volume you're currently doing. Be honest about what you offer.

items: Attend local REIA meetings monthly to meet potential partners and contractors
Post detailed job listings on Indeed, LinkedIn, and Craigslist for acquisitions roles
Use referrals — ask your title company or attorney who else they work with
Test VAs through Upwork or OnlineJobs.ph with a paid trial task before committing
Join real estate investor Facebook groups to find active dispositions partners
Look for former mortgage or insurance sales reps for acquisitions positions

sections.content: When to Hire: A Simple Framework

A common mistake is hiring too early and draining cash before deals justify it. A simple rule: hire when a role is costing you deals or costing you hours that directly limit your income. If you're missing follow-up calls because you're drowning in paperwork, hire a VA. If deals are dying because no one is pushing them to close, hire a TC. Use your [Deal Calculator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) to figure out what your average deal nets you, then ask yourself: would one extra deal per month pay for this hire? If yes, make the move.

Also think carefully about how each team member affects your exit options. A stronger team means you can hold, sell, or assign more deals with confidence. Understanding your options is key — the guide on [Exit Strategies: When to Hold, Sell, or 1031](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/real-estate-investor-exit-strategies) is a useful read when planning your overall business model.

Pro Tip: Document every process before you delegate it. Write a short SOP (Standard Operating Procedure) for each task. This makes training faster, reduces errors, and means you're not the only person who knows how something works.
Team Structure by Stage

Here's a rough guide to how your team should look at different stages. If you're brand new, start with [Real Estate Investing for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners) or [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) before worrying about team structure.

items: 0 to 2 deals/month: Solo or with a VA — focus on lead gen and your first closings
2 to 5 deals/month: Add a part-time acquisitions rep and a transaction coordinator
5 to 10 deals/month: Bring on a full-time acquisitions manager and a dispo rep
10+ deals/month: Add operations manager, marketing manager, and dedicated TC

sections.content: This is not a rigid ladder. Some investors hire a dispo partner before an acquisitions manager. Others outsource everything except seller calls. There's no single right answer, but there is a wrong answer: trying to do it all alone when your deal flow outpaces your capacity.
